title: A-H-V

lines: THEY SEEMED BUT A FEW DAYS.
FOR THE LOVE HE HAD TO HER.
cards: Seven years is a long time to work for anyone. Jacob agrees to it, working for his uncle Laban, so that he can marry Laban's daughter Rachel. Seven years of flocks, heat and cold nights.

And the Torah sums it all up in one sentence: "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Years that felt like days. That's what love did to the clock.
The word for love in that verse is today's root.

teach.b: A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet. Ahavah, love.
Four verses, four loves. First, love strong enough to bend time. That's Jacob.
The Torah doesn't hide that this kind of love is real, and that it can change how a whole life feels. Second, love as a command.
"And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might."
Those words follow straight after the Shema, and they raise a question teachers have asked: how can anyone be commanded to feel something?
One answer the tradition gives: in the Torah, love is also something you do, with your heart, your soul and your might, which is to say with your whole life.
"Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Tradition says Rabbi Akiva called this verse a great principle of the Torah. Fourth, later in the same chapter, the stranger.
"Thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The same words, as thyself, now aimed at the outsider, with a reason: you know what it's like.
So one root holds a young man's longing, a whole people's devotion, the person next door, and the immigrant down the road.
Ahavah isn't kept for the ones who are easy to love. In every one of these verses, it's a word you can say and a thing you can do.

how: The paragraph beginning 'and thou shalt love the LORD thy God' is said right after the first line of the Shema, morning and evening, and the blessing just before the Shema speaks of God's love for Israel.

o: a desire or longing that is never acted on
the loyalty a servant owes to a master
love: felt, and also done, for God and people

games.q: who is loved — tap the pairs.
p: seven years that seemed a few days
for ye were strangers in Egypt

s: the Torah commands love for the stranger, not only the neighbor
"thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."
Jacob's seven years felt endless to him
"they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her."
the command to love God comes right after the Shema
"and thou shalt love the LORD thy God" follows straight on.

games.q: you're Jacob. Laban asks what your wages should be. you love Rachel. what do you offer?
o: to work seven years for Rachel.
to pay a bride price in silver.
to take Rachel and leave that night.
games.why: Jacob offers seven years' work, and the years seemed but a few days, for the love he had to her.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love and don't often say it to: a parent, a friend, a sibling, a child who's grown. See their face, and on each breath out, say silently, I love you.
If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, by name.

wordCard.voice: A-H-V. Alef, hey, vet: ahavah, love. For Rachel, for God, for the neighbor, and for the stranger. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: love; from the root alef, hey, vet.

carryVoice: Your line: ahavah. In the Torah, love is felt, and it's also done. That's another day up the hill.
